I am 63 years old, and I have worked these fields in Quzhou for 40 years. My wife and I are the only labor left on our 15 mu, so I must plan with our backs in mind. I know this soil, and I know what it can give me if I do not get greedy.

I will put 10 mu into my wheat-maize rotation. That is my foundation — wheat keeps us fed, and maize brings steady money. I sow improved wheat in October, after rotary tilling and spreading basal compound fertilizer. My well is my lifeline, so I irrigate four times: once before winter to protect the seedlings from the cold, once at jointing when the spring warms up, once at heading, and once at grain filling. I spray herbicide once and insecticide twice — that is enough if you walk the fields every morning. I topdress with urea at jointing. With good weather, I expect about 950 jin of wheat per mu.

After harvest in early June, I sow hybrid maize the same week. I do not till — I plant straight into the wheat stubble. That saves me precious days and diesel, and the stubble mulch keeps moisture in the ground. Maize is simpler: two irrigations, one when it reaches my knee and one at grain filling, plus three pesticide applications. Hybrid seed costs more, but it pays me back — I have seen over 1000 jin per mu on this land before.

The remaining 5 mu I plant with cotton. Cotton is heavy work — hand picking, many sprays — but the price at the gin is better than grain. I plant hybrid Bt cotton in late April after rotary tilling. I irrigate three times and spray five times total. The Bt gene helps with bollworm, so I do not need the 15 sprays we used to do. I fertilize with compound and a side-dressing of urea when it flowers. I expect about 500 jin of seed cotton per mu.

I have learned that fertilizer is not a place to save money, but I also do not throw it away. Compound fertilizer goes down at sowing for all three crops, and I topdress wheat and cotton with urea when they need it most. That is my plan.
